newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka's ruling alliance sweeps local polls.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka's ruling alliance sweeps local polls.

text.p: Sri Lankan President Chandrika Kumaratunga's ruling People's Alliance (PA) swept to a landslide victory in local polls on Saturday in its first political test since taking power in 1994.
Elections Commissioner Dayananda Dissanayake said the PA won 194 councils and the main opposition United National Party (UNP) 43 of the 238 local bodies at stake in Friday's election.
One local council was won by an independent group.

Dissanayake said on state television that PA received 49 percent of the total votes polled in Friday's election against UNP's 41.25 percent. The rest was split between smaller parties and independent groups.
The local polls were widely seen as a mid-term appraisal of President Chandrika Kumaratunga's government after it won power two and a half years ago, ending UNP's 17 year rule.

Their outcome may influence future government decisions, such as putting a peace plan, aimed at ending a war with Tamil separatists in the north, to a vote. The war, which has cost thousands of lives, was, however, not a direct issue in the poll.
The state radio quoted the PA general secretary D.M. Jayaratne as saying that the landslide victory was unexpected.
The PA received another mandate from the people approving its two-and-a-half-year administration and the "the administration would consolidate on this victory," he added.
Political sources said while the PA had improved its position in the island's rural areas it was mostly rejected by voters in the urban centres, including capital Colombo.
"The minority vote in Colombo seems to have swung the UNP's way. We expected a different outcome in Colombo," government minister A.H.M. Fowzie, PA's campaign manager for Colombo, told Reuters.
"Colombo's importance cannot be underrated given that it is the nerve centre of the economy," said political analyst Dayan Jayatilake.
"Also given that most of Colombo's voters are from the minorities, the UNP scored a strategic victory there," said Jayatilake, who is editor of the Lanka Guardian magazine.
The government is currently in the midst of launching contitutional reforms that aim to give more powers to the Tamil and Moslem minorities.
But other analysts said the government can take credit for its performance outside Colombo, where it won 176 of the 195 village concils that were up for grabs.
"The election showed overwhelming support for the PA from the rural sector," said a Tamil political analyst who declined to be identified.
"Over the past two-and-a-half years, the government has gone to the grassroots with its peace message and it seems that the grassroots have accepted that message," he said.
Opposition leader and former prime minister Ranil Wickremesinghe accused the goverment of rigging the elections and said the UNP would take legal action against it.
"There have been massive rigging by PA," he told Reuters.
"We are certainly going to make it a major issue in the country. Our lawyers are right now looking at it and we will be taking appropriate legal action," he said.
But Dissanayake said that polling was fair.
He said 77 percent of some 10 million eligible voters had cast ballots in the election, up from 61 percent in the previous 1991 local polls.
The Elections Department earlier said 65 percent of the eligible voters had cast their ballots.
It said voter turnout was moderate early on Friday but had picked up later in the day.
Elections were not held in the country's northern and eastern provinces where government troops are fighting the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam.
